title: Podcasting
desc: Plan, record, edit, publish and grow a podcast with good audio, honest rights, and a simple way to earn.
outcomes: Explain formats, audiences and the production chain.
Record clean audio and edit with free tools.
task: Plan and publish a three-episode podcast season with show plan, scripts, clean audio, show notes, rights check and listener review.
condition: A phone or mic, free editing software, a quiet room, two peers and a mentor.
standard: Audio is clear with steady levels; every episode has notes and a rights check; episodes publish on a free host; listener data reviewed; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Creators, teachers, small businesses, community groups.
evidence: show plan, 3 episodes, show notes, rights sheet, review
modules: Concept, audience and promise
Understand
A podcast succeeds when one kind of listener knows exactly what they will get. Start with that promise, not with equipment.
Write the promise in one sentence: "For [listener], this show gives [benefit] every [time] in [length]".
Listen to five shows in your topic. Note length, format, opening, and what you would do differently.
Choose a format that suits you: solo talk, interview, story, panel or news. Interviews need guest management; solo shows need discipline.
Choose a schedule you can keep for 20 episodes, not 5.
"For small farmers, this show gives one tested tip every Monday in 12 minutes." The host can now say no to topics that do not fit and a listener can decide in ten seconds.
Write your one-sentence promise, a 5-line show plan (format, length, schedule, first six episode ideas) and a listener profile.
Promise names listener, benefit, rhythm and length; six episode ideas fit the promise.
Scripting and structure
Create
A script keeps you short and clear. It need not be word for word, but the opening and closing should be written out.
Structure: hook (under 30 seconds), context, body in 2 or 3 points, one action, sign-off.
Write for the ear: short sentences, everyday words, one idea per sentence.
Use signposts such as "first", "second" and "last" so listeners can follow.
Time yourself reading aloud; speaking runs about 140 words per minute.
A 12-minute episode needs about 1,600 words. The host writes 250 words for the opening and first point, bullet notes for the middle, and a written closing of 100 words.
Script your first episode and time it by reading aloud.
Script runs within 10 per cent of the target length and has a hook and an action.
Recording clean audio
Apply
Clean sound matters more than expensive microphones.
Record in a small room with soft surfaces: curtains, rugs, a wardrobe of clothes or blankets.
Keep the mic 10 to 15 cm from your mouth and speak slightly across it to reduce harsh sounds.
Use headphones to monitor; keep peaks below the red zone and record a few seconds of room tone.
Switch off fans, phones and fridge noise; record a backup copy.
Recording moves from a bare kitchen to a bedroom with a mattress against one wall. Echo falls so much that the editor needs no special filter.
Record a 2-minute test in two rooms and compare.
Chosen recording has steady level, little noise and no clipping.
Editing and sound quality
Apply
Editing is mostly deleting. Free software is enough.
Remove long pauses, false starts, repeated words and loud breaths; keep natural rhythm.
Apply gentle noise reduction and a limiter; avoid heavy effects.
Match loudness between episodes and check on phone speakers and earbuds.
Export in a standard format and keep the project file as backup.
A 20-minute raw recording becomes a 14-minute episode after cutting two tangents and four false starts. Loudness is set to the same level as the last episode.
Edit your first episode and keep before and after files.
Edited episode is within target length and sounds equal in level start to finish.
Rights, consent and ethics
Evaluate
Respecting rights keeps your show alive and your guests safe.
Do not use popular music without a licence. Use music you made or music with a licence that allows podcast use, and credit as required.
Short quotes may be allowed in some places; check the rule and give credit.
Get a guest's spoken and written consent to record and publish.
Do not publish private information, defamatory claims or misleading advice.
A host records a one-line consent at the start ("Do you agree that this interview can be published?") and stores a signed note with the files.
Complete a rights sheet for one episode: music, quotes, guest consent and images.
Every item has a source or permission and a date.
Publishing and promoting
Apply
Publishing is a repeatable routine.
Write a clear title, a three-sentence description and time stamps.
Upload audio to a podcast host and submit the feed link to listening apps once.
Make a square cover image that is readable at small size.
Share short clips, quotes or questions on a platform where your listeners are.
Episodes are released on Monday at 6 am so they are ready for commuters. A 30-second clip with captions brings new listeners.
Publish a trailer or first episode and a checklist for each release.
Episode is live in at least one app and the checklist is complete.
Listener data and improvement
Analyse
Numbers show where listeners lose interest.
Look at downloads, listen-through rate and drop-off points.
Ask for feedback with one question: what would you change?
Change one thing per episode so you can see the effect.
Keep a simple results table.
Retention falls at minute 8 in four episodes. The host moves the long interview later and shortens the intro; retention improves by 10 per cent.
Write three findings and one test for the next three episodes.
Findings are based on numbers and the test is measurable.
Earning, sustaining and growing
Evaluate
A podcast earns slowly and honestly.
Income sources: sponsors, listener support, courses, services and events.
Disclose sponsors at the start of the episode.
Plan a calendar and batch-record to avoid burn-out.
Review quarterly: keep, change or stop.
A show with 800 listeners per episode earns from a local sponsor at a flat monthly fee and a paid mini-course. The host records four episodes in one day each month.
Write a six-month plan with release calendar, income goal and review date.
Plan shows realistic numbers and a review date.
quiz: Hook purpose?
Capture attention. (Covered in module 2: Scripting and structure. To pass that module: Script runs within 10 per cent of the target length and has a hook and an action.)
Clipping?
Distorted loud peaks. (Covered in module 3: Recording clean audio. To pass that module: Chosen recording has steady level, little noise and no clipping.)
Mic distance?
About a hand width. (Covered in module 3: Recording clean audio. To pass that module: Chosen recording has steady level, little noise and no clipping.)
Rights rule?
Use only what you may. (Covered in module 5: Rights, consent and ethics. To pass that module: Every item has a source or permission and a date.)
Guest consent?
Required. (Covered in module 5: Rights, consent and ethics. To pass that module: Every item has a source or permission and a date.)
Drop-off?
Where listeners leave. (Covered in module 7: Listener data and improvement. To pass that module: Findings are based on numbers and the test is measurable.)
Sponsor rule?
Disclose. (Covered in module 8: Earning, sustaining and growing. To pass that module: Plan shows realistic numbers and a review date.)
Why room tone?
Fix gaps. (Covered in module 3: Recording clean audio. To pass that module: Chosen recording has steady level, little noise and no clipping.)
Show notes use?
Search and clarity. (Covered in module 6: Publishing and promoting. To pass that module: Episode is live in at least one app and the checklist is complete.)
Free host?
Distributes feed. (Covered in module 6: Publishing and promoting. To pass that module: Episode is live in at least one app and the checklist is complete.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
Checked, dated and explained to others
